analysis.one_liner: Lets voters force a floor vote on any bill by signing a national petition.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: after its sponsor introduced it in June 2018, no other member signed on and the two committees it was sent to took no action before the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new way for the public to break a Congressional logjam. If the sponsor of a stuck bill requests it, the House Clerk and Senate Secretary would post an online national petition for that bill. Once at least 5 million registered voters nationwide sign it — with no more than a quarter from any one state — and the bill has at least 50 House cosponsors (or 11 senators) plus a budget or research analysis, chamber leaders would be required to schedule a vote on final passage within 15 days. Signers' names would be kept confidential.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters who support a bill that Congressional leadership refuses to bring to the floor. It also helps individual members of Congress whose bills are stalled by their own party's leaders, and makes it easier for any registered voter to register by linking from the petition site.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters backing bills stalled by leaders

how_it_helps.text: The bill states in its findings that Congressional leadership and individual members have repeatedly blocked votes on matters a majority of the public supports, and that this refusal prevents deliberation even when a majority of Congress favors a bill [S3].

Once a petition passes the threshold, the Speaker or Senate Majority Leader must schedule a vote on final passage within 15 working days, removing the leaders' ability to keep the bill off the floor indefinitely [S3].

The Clerk and Secretary would make petitions available for signature by online methods, making the process accessible to ordinary voters rather than only to members of Congress, who alone can use the existing House discharge petition [S3].
The bill requires the petition websites to provide a link where anyone can learn how to register to vote in their state [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Congressional party leaders, who would lose their power to keep popular bills from ever getting a vote; taxpayers fund the Clerk's and Secretary's new signature-gathering and verification system.

drawbacks.text: The trigger is very high: 5 million verified signatures, a cap so no single state supplies more than a quarter of them, plus 50 House cosponsors or 11 senators and a completed CBO or CRS analysis [S3]. That combination could be nearly impossible to reach for many popular bills, since the 50-cosponsor requirement can itself be blocked by the same leaders the bill targets.

Forcing a vote on any bill that clears the thresholds could push complex legislation to the floor quickly — within 15 days — with limited committee vetting, which is the standard criticism of the existing discharge petition process [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea addresses a real imbalance: a handful of chamber leaders can bury bills supported by a public majority and even by most members. But this version's stacked thresholds — 5 million signatures, a state cap, 50 cosponsors, and an analysis requirement — make the escape hatch narrow, and it never received even a committee hearing, so there was no chance to test or refine it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration and Rules Committees on the day it was introduced, no one else cosponsored it, and it died there when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Raul Ruiz introduced the bill in the House on June 28, 2018 [S1].
It was referred the same day to the Committee on House Administration and to the Committee on Rules [S5].
No further action was taken before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so the bill never received a committee hearing or a floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Congressional leaders and committee chairs keep the sole power to decide which bills get a vote, and no outside group is worse off. The status quo — where leadership can indefinitely block bills the public supports — is preserved.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never tested.

industries.industry: Congressional party leaders and committee chairs
industries.note: The bill would strip leaders of their power to keep bills off the floor once a public petition and a bloc of cosponsors trigger it. Its findings directly charge that leadership has blocked votes on matters a public majority supports.

Today, groups wanting a stalled bill considered must persuade chamber leaders and committee chairs; a public petition route would add a channel that bypasses those gatekeepers. The bill's high signature and cosponsor thresholds, however, would leave most of the existing access structure intact.
